Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: Rural Ghana police stations predominantly use paper-based records for case files, complaints, and incidents. Key evidence: Local stations record on paper files (easily lost), lack modern technology especially in smaller towns/hinterlands; records physically transported to Accra CID HQ for central database (no remote sync). CDSB receives crime details on paper CID Forms 6/8 from stations. Ongoing central digitization of old records partial (AFIS 2011, but only 3700 fingerprints captured). Recent central services digitized (e.g., clearance 2023), but no evidence of station-level digital case recording. New IPDMS (2025) promoted but appears promotional/pilot, not rolled out to rural. Academic study (2023) confirms manual processes; hinterland data rarely included nationally. Score 1: entirely paper-based at rural facilities, digitized later centrally.

revision_notes: Cited CDSB source fetched and confirmed directly; the original sagepub source returned a 403 error on fetch and could not be re-verified, and the JCU repository source was not re-checked. A fresh search covering 2024-2025 finds no evidence that rural police stations have moved beyond paper-based case recording: the Criminal Data Service Bureau still receives paper CID Forms 6/8 from stations, only around 3,700 fingerprint records have been digitised centrally via AFIS, and 2024-2025 initiatives (an AI-powered Real-Time Crime Centre, community policing technology studies, GIS policing research) are concentrated in Accra/major regions or remain at proposal/pilot stage with no rural station-level rollout. Score of 1 (Entirely paper) confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural police stations in Ghana continue to rely on paper-based case files and CID Forms 6 and 8 for recording complaints and incidents, which are physically transported to the Criminal Investigations Department in Accra for later digitisation into the Automated Fingerprint Identification System (AFIS) and Criminal Records Database. Only a small fraction of historical records (around 3,700 fingerprint sets) has been digitised centrally, and national initiatives such as the planned AI-powered Real-Time Crime Centre (announced 2025) and the Integrated Police Data Management System remain concentrated in Accra with no evidence of rollout to rural stations. Studies of community policing technology use in Ghana (2024) find that officers rely mainly on personal mobile phones rather than dedicated digital case-management systems, constrained by financial limitations and low digital literacy, particularly outside major urban centres.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Ghana, particularly CHPS compounds, predominantly use paper-based registers for patient data recording at point of care. Aggregate data is compiled monthly on paper tallies and entered into DHIMS2 (DHIS2) at district level for national reporting.PLOS Digital Health Patient-level EHR like LHIMS is standard in district/regional hospitals and urban facilities in 16 regional capitals, with ongoing efforts to extend to health centers, but not yet rolled out to most rural clinics.[Same] In a semi-rural district, only two hospitals used EHR while "the rest are all health centers that rely on paper records."Digital Health journal Pilots like Simprints biometrics exist in select rural CHPS (e.g., 325 Eastern Region facilities), but represent isolated donor projects.[Global Citizen] Barriers include unreliable rural electricity/internet, low digital literacy (esp. older managers), staff turnover, training gaps, and interoperability issues between DHIMS/LHIMS. National policy (2023-2027 Digital Health Strategy) aims for digital transformation, but rural POC lags behind urban/secondary care and aggregate systems, with paper default.WHO-extranet policy

Cross-referenced with three additional 2025 studies: a Savannah Region case report on DHIS2 e-Tracker rollout to CHPS compounds (partial, inconsistent uptake even among enrolled facilities), a Northern Ghana CHPS study, and an Ashanti semi-rural EHR survey confirming health centres rely on paper records while only hospitals use EHR. All confirm paper-based recording remains the norm at rural facility level with only partial, donor-supported digital pilots. Score of 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Ghana, particularly Community-based Health Planning and Services (CHPS) compounds, predominantly record patient data on paper registers and tally sheets at the point of care. Aggregate figures are subsequently entered into the District Health Information Management System 2 (DHIMS2) at facility or district level. Point-of-care electronic tools such as the DHIS2 e-Tracker have been piloted in selected regions (for example Savannah Region from 2023), but uptake even within pilot facilities is partial and inconsistent, and 2025 studies confirm that most rural health centres continue to rely on paper records, with electronic health record systems concentrated in district and regional hospitals rather than rural facilities.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Ghana predominantly use paper-based recording for births, with forms filled manually at local points and later aggregated or scanned for electronic transmission to district/regional/central levels, as per traditional structure under Act 301/1027 and UNECA assessment listing Ghana for electronic transmission but not full district-wide digitalization at point-of-service [Journal of Public Health in Africa study]. Digital pilots like m-Birth (UNICEF-supported since 2017) enable some electronic capture via mobile in rural/remote areas, but coverage is limited by infrastructure/connectivity gaps, benefiting urban more than rural, with persistent urban-rural disparities (64-70% rural registration vs 80% urban) [Int J Pediatrics 2025]. Barriers include poor electricity/internet in rural areas, low staffing/resources, geographical access issues, and incomplete rollout beyond pilots/outreach. National ambitions (Act 1027 decentralization/digitalization, CRVS plans) outpace rural reality, where paper remains default with digital for aggregate reporting/pilots [UNECA CRVS Digitalization report].

revision_notes: Original UNECA assessment source fetched and confirmed general picture; one cited PMC link was blocked by a bot-check on direct fetch. Fresh search finds a major national reform, the Ghana Card Number at Birth System (launched March 2024), which links health-facility birth records electronically to the Births and Deaths Registry and National Identification Authority, but the Registry's own 2025-2030 CRVS Strategic Plan (validated July 2025) identifies 'expanding mobile registration in remote areas' as a forward priority, indicating rural offices have not yet made this transition, and a 2025 peer-reviewed review confirms digitalisation gains have favoured urban over rural areas owing to persistent infrastructure gaps. Score of 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices in Ghana record births primarily on paper forms at the point of service, with data subsequently compiled and, where infrastructure allows, transmitted electronically to district, regional and national databases. Digital tools such as the m-Birth mobile platform and the Ghana Card Number at Birth System (launched March 2024, linking the Ghana Health Service, the Births and Deaths Registry and the National Identification Authority) have extended some electronic capture to births occurring in health facilities with adequate connectivity. However, the Births and Deaths Registry's own 2025-2030 CRVS Strategic Plan identifies expansion of mobile registration to remote areas as a forward priority, and current academic literature confirms that digitalisation gains have disproportionately benefited urban over rural areas owing to persistent infrastructure and connectivity constraints.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Ghana predominantly use paper-based recording for administrative data, attendance, and learning outcomes, such as manual registers and annual census questionnaires completed by head teachers. These paper forms are forwarded to district and regional offices for data entry and aggregation into the national EMIS, with no routine digital entry at the point of service in most rural facilities.World Bank EMIS Ghana Digital systems like the GES EMIS mobile app for annual census data entry exist and are promoted for teachers, but daily attendance remains paper-based. Pilots such as mSRC app (2014, 20 districts) and GALOP project laptops for weekly attendance uploads represent isolated donor/Gov initiatives, not standard across rural Ghana. Recent studies (2025) show rural headteachers use basic digital tools (spreadsheets 50%, email 50%) inconsistently due to infrastructure gaps (internet, electricity, hardware).GSCARR ICT Study Barriers include poor connectivity, low IT capacity, teacher training deficits, and resource scarcity in rural areas vs. urban. National EMIS ambition contrasts with rural paper reality, where data is transcribed higher up.UEW Record Keeping Thesis

A 2024 Global Partnership for Education programme document confirms EMIS was digitised in 2022 but functions primarily as an annual census/aggregate reporting tool rather than day-to-day facility-level data capture, with daily attendance and mSRC reporting still transitioning from paper. The GSCARR 2025 Wenchi Municipality study confirms inconsistent ICT use by rural headteachers for administrative tasks despite the One-Teacher-One-Laptop programme, with a marked urban-rural divide driven by infrastructure gaps. Score of 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) confirmed.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Ghana predominantly use paper-based registers for day-to-day administrative data such as attendance, with head teachers completing an annual EMIS census (digitised since 2022) that is entered via a mobile app or web platform at a later point rather than captured digitally at the moment of use. Digital tools including the mobile School Report Card (mSRC) exist to support weekly reporting, but a 2025 study of rural headteachers in the Wenchi Municipality found that use of ICT for administrative and data-management tasks remains inconsistent and significantly behind urban schools, constrained by infrastructure gaps in electricity, internet connectivity and hardware.
